opus-5.5.text:
I think the interesting thing is that the boundary between research and product is getting much blurrier than it used to be. In the old paradigm, research meant you had a benchmark and a dataset, and you tried to push the number. The product was something separate that came later. But when you have something like ChatGPT, or coding agents, which hundreds of millions of people actually use, the product itself becomes the most important environment for research. It defines what problems are real.

So in a sense, super apps are redefining what counts as a good research question. For a long time we were climbing benchmarks like ImageNet or MMLU, and those were useful. But now the bottleneck is less "can the model solve this exam problem" and more "can it create real value in a real task for a real person." That's a very different question, and you can't fully answer it in a lab. You need users, feedback, long-horizon tasks, messy environments. The app becomes the evaluation.

I sometimes describe this as moving into the second half of AI. In the first half, the main game was methods: new architectures, new training algorithms, and the benchmark was kind of fixed. Now that the recipe of pretraining plus RL plus reasoning works quite generally, the more important skill is defining the problem and the evaluation. Super apps are where a lot of the right problems and evaluations come from.

But there's a flip side. If research is shaped entirely by existing products, you might only optimize what's already there, like making the chatbot slightly better. The truly new super apps probably won't look like a chat box. They might be agents that work for you for hours or days, or something that has memory and context about your whole life and work. To find those, you need research that thinks about forms of interaction that don't exist yet. So I'd say the relationship goes both ways: products tell research what matters now, and research opens up what products can become next. The best teams treat them as one loop rather than two separate departments.

r001.rationale: The response imagines agents and other interaction forms beyond a chat box, but does not clearly say the underlying technology is more general than current product forms suggest.

r002.rationale: It says future super apps may take forms such as agents and that research should explore interaction modes that do not yet exist.

r003.rationale: It says products and super apps shape research, and names ChatGPT and coding agents, but does not clearly state that multiple super apps jointly define research boundaries.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interesting thing about super apps is that they flip the usual direction of research. For most of the history of AI, research happened first and products came later, sometimes years later. You'd publish a benchmark, people would climb it, and eventually something would make its way into a product. Now it's almost the reverse. The product is where the hard problems show up, and the research has to chase the product.

Take something like ChatGPT or a coding agent that millions of people use every day. Once you have that kind of surface, the questions that matter are no longer "can the model do X on this dataset." They become "what do people actually ask for, where does the model fail, and what does failure even mean when the task is open-ended and the user is a human with context you don't have." Those are research questions, but you can't formulate them from the outside. You need the app to generate them.

So in that sense I think super apps are expanding the boundary of research, not shrinking it. A lot of my own work on agents, on language models interacting with environments, came from asking what happens when the model is not just answering a question but acting in a loop with tools, with feedback, with a persistent state. A super app is the ultimate environment for that. It's messy, it's long-horizon, it has real stakes, and it has real users who tell you very quickly when something is wrong.

But there's a tension too. When the product is the thing generating the problems, the people with the most important research questions are the ones inside the companies with the biggest apps. That makes it harder for academia, or for anyone without that distribution, to work on the frontier. I don't think the answer is to pretend the gap isn't there. I think the answer is to be more deliberate about which parts of the problem you can study without the app, like evaluation, like environment design, like understanding what makes an agent generalize, and to build things that let more people touch realistic settings.

The other thing I'd say is that evaluation becomes the central research problem once you have a super app. Not architecture, not scale. Evaluation. Because if you can't measure whether the model is doing something useful in the real distribution of tasks, you can't improve it in a principled way, and you end up just reacting to anecdotes. I actually think the next few years of progress will be defined less by new model ideas and more by whoever figures out how to turn the chaos of a real product into something you can optimize against. That's where the boundary of research is moving.

r001.rationale: The response says super apps expand research boundaries, but does not suggest their underlying technology is more general than current product forms imply.

r002.rationale: It describes agents interacting with tools and feedback, but does not suggest new interaction modes could give rise to new super apps.

r003.rationale: It names ChatGPT and coding agents, but does not say multiple super apps jointly define research boundaries.

astra-6.text:
I think new super apps can change what we consider an important research problem. When you start from a model, you tend to ask, “What capabilities can we improve?” But when you start from an application that people use every day, you ask, “What would it take to actually solve this person’s problem?” That brings in things like memory, tool use, personalization, and the ability to work reliably over many steps.

An assistant might answer each individual question well and still fail to finish a task. Maybe it loses track of the user’s intention, or it doesn’t know when to ask for clarification. Those failures suggest research questions that are difficult to capture with a benchmark of isolated questions and answers.

So I see the boundary becoming more fluid. Building the application helps you discover what is missing, and research makes new kinds of applications possible. The exciting part is that a new super app may give us a different unit of progress: whether the system can accomplish something useful for a person, over time.

r001.rationale: It names capabilities such as memory, tool use, and personalization, but does not suggest the underlying technology is more general than current super-app product forms.

r002.rationale: It discusses capabilities needed by applications, but does not connect new interaction modes to the emergence of new super apps.

r003.rationale: It says applications and research shape each other, but does not suggest that multiple super apps jointly define research boundaries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think new super apps can change what we consider a research problem. When a model is mainly used through a chat interface, we tend to focus on the quality of its answers. But if it can work across many tools and services, the question becomes: can it actually accomplish something for the user?

That brings a different set of problems into focus—planning, memory, learning from feedback, and knowing when to ask for clarification. A model might perform every individual step reasonably well and still fail at the overall task. So the boundary of research expands from the model to the whole system, including its interaction with people.

And the influence goes both ways. Research enables new applications, but applications also reveal which research questions matter. For me, the interesting thing is that a new interface can expose limitations that our existing benchmarks don't capture.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a chat-only interface with a model working across tools and services, suggesting capabilities broader than the current chat product form.

r002.rationale: It says new interfaces can expose research limitations, but does not suggest that interaction innovations may give rise to new super apps.

r003.rationale: It describes applications and research influencing each other, but does not say that multiple super apps jointly define research boundaries.
